overview.text: The natural logarithm, written ln x, is the logarithm to base e: it answers the question “to what power must e be raised to produce x?” For positive x, it can also be defined by the integral ln x = ∫₁ˣ (1/t) dt, making its value the signed area under y = 1/t between 1 and x. This definition explains its key calculus role: its derivative is 1/x, so an antiderivative of 1/x is ln|x| + C on any interval that does not cross zero. The number e is characterized by ln e = 1, and ln is the inverse of the exponential function eˣ.

key_facts.text: ln x is the logarithm of x to base e, where e is approximately 2.71828.
For x > 0, ln x = ∫₁ˣ (1/t) dt; when 0 < x < 1, this integral is negative.
For x > 0, the derivative of ln x is 1/x.
For x ≠ 0, an antiderivative of 1/x is ln|x| + C; the absolute value allows the formula on negative intervals too.
The number e is characterized by ln e = 1, and the natural logarithm and exponential function are inverses.
